summary.text: The proof first shows that every positive nonzero quadratic nonresidue modulo \(7\) is represented by \((3C^2+7B^2+14A^2)/8\): Dirichlet primes and quadratic reciprocity produce locally soluble auxiliary diagonal forms, while lattice enlargement and reduction force a minimal-discriminant ternary form into the required class. For large \(n\), a residue argument selects two nearby admissible coordinate sums \(s\), and the ternary representation of \((14n-7s-3s^2)/6\) converts to two distinct nonnegative representations; explicit witness tables cover \(42\le n<4900\), and exhaustive bounded counting handles \(n\le41\).

full_proof.text:
Put
\[
 P(u)=\frac{u(3u+1)}2\qquad(u\in\mathbb N).
\]
Let \(a(n)\) be the number of quadruples \((x,y,z,w)\in\mathbb N^4\) such that
\[
 x\le y,\qquad n=P(x)+P(y)+2P(z)+3P(w).                 \tag{1}
\]
We prove that every \(n>5\) has such a representation and that the values represented exactly once are precisely
\[
 E=\{0,2,7,9,11,12,16,31,33,41\}.
\]
In fact, we shall prove the stronger assertion \(a(n)\ge2\) for every \(n\ge42\).

The main ingredient is the following ternary theorem.

**Ternary representation theorem.** If \(m>0\), if \(7\nmid m\), and if the residue of \(m\) modulo \(7\) is one of \(3,5,6\), then there are integers \(A,B,C\) such that
\[
 3C^2+7B^2+14A^2=8m.                                  \tag{2}
\]

We first prove this theorem. The somewhat lengthy proof is included because it is what makes the later construction uniform.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1. Reduction of ternary quadratic forms

Write an integral ternary quadratic form as
\[
 F(X,Y,Z)=aX^2+bY^2+cZ^2+dYZ+eXZ+fXY
\]
and define
\[
 \Delta(F)=4abc+def-ad^2-be^2-cf^2.                    \tag{3}
\]
Thus twice \(\Delta(F)\) is the determinant of the Hessian matrix of \(F\). Under a nonsingular rational change of variables \(T\),
\[
 \Delta(F\circ T)=\Delta(F)(\det T)^2.                 \tag{4}
\]

Call \(F\) reduced if
\[
\begin{gathered}
0<a\le b\le c,
\quad 0\le e\le a,
\quad 0\le f\le a,
\quad -b\le d\le b,\\
e+f-d\le a+b.                                             \tag{5}
\end{gathered}
\]
For every reduced form,
\[
 2abc\le \Delta(F).                                    \tag{6}
\]
Here is the elementary inequality behind (6). Put \(u=f,v=e,w=|d|\). If \(d\ge0\), the restrictions in (5) imply
\[
 aw^2+bv^2+cu^2-uvw\le2abc.
\]
One proves this successively from
\[
\begin{aligned}
cu^2-uvw&\le a(ca-vw),\\
bv^2-avw&\le a^2(b-w),\\
aw^2+a^2b-a^2w&\le ab^2,\\
ab^2+ca^2&\le2abc.
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(d<0\), (5) gives \(u+v+w\le a+b\), and
\[
 aw^2+bv^2+cu^2+uvw\le2abc.
\]
For this, first replace \(c\) by \(b\); the resulting inequality follows by separating the cases \(u+v\le a\) and \(u+v\ge a\), using
\[
 b(u^2+v^2)+uvw=b(u+v)^2-(2b-w)uv.
\]
The excess \((c-b)u^2\) is then absorbed using \(u^2\le ab\). Substitution in (3) gives (6).

We need a standard minimal-form argument, which we spell out. Fix a positive definite rational form \(G\) and an integer \(m\). Call an integral form \(F\) admissible if it is rationally equivalent to \(G\) and represents \(m\). Among all admissible forms choose first one with least positive discriminant; among those choose one with least \(a\), then least \(b\), then least \(c\). Such successive minima exist because all four quantities are positive integers.

Integral unimodular substitutions preserve admissibility and discriminant. Comparing the chosen form with the forms obtained by interchanging variables and by replacing one variable by its sum or difference with another gives
\[
0<a\le b\le c,
\quad |e|,|f|\le a,
\quad |d|\le b,
\quad e+f-d\le a+b.
\]
Changing signs of \(Y\) and \(Z\), without changing the diagonal coefficients, makes \(e,f\ge0\). Thus an admissible reduced form exists.

We next record the local consequence of minimality. Say that \(F\) has a primitive zero modulo \(p^k\) if there is an integral vector \(v\), not all of whose coordinates are divisible by \(p\), with
\[
 p^k\mid F(v).
\]
If a minimal admissible \(F\) has a primitive zero modulo \(p^2\), then
\[
 p^2\nmid\Delta(F).                                    \tag{7}
\]
Also, for every odd prime \(p\),
\[
 p^3\nmid\Delta(F).                                    \tag{8}
\]

For completeness, these facts follow from an integral-overlattice argument. Let \(H\) be the Hessian of \(F\). If a primitive \(v\) satisfies \(p^2\mid F(v)\) and \(p\mid Hv\), use a unimodular change of basis to make one unit coordinate of \(v\) the first coordinate. The transformed form then has its first diagonal coefficient divisible by \(p^2\) and both cross-coefficients involving the first variable divisible by \(p\). Dividing that variable by \(p\) therefore gives another integral admissible form whose discriminant is \(\Delta(F)/p^2\), contradicting minimality.

If instead \(Hv\not\equiv0\pmod p\), complete \(v\) to a basis modulo \(p\). In this basis the Hessian has one nonzero entry in its first row. The assumptions \(F(v)\equiv0\pmod {p^2}\) and \(p^2\mid\Delta(F)\) yield another primitive vector whose norm is divisible by \(p^2\) and whose gradient is divisible by \(p\), reducing to the previous contradiction. This proves (7).

For (8), if every value of \(F\) is divisible by \(p\), divide all six coefficients by \(p\); a nontrivial zero modulo \(p\) of the quotient exists because every ternary quadratic form over the odd finite field \(\mathbb F_p\) is isotropic. Multiplying back gives a primitive vector with norm divisible by \(p^2\) and gradient divisible by \(p\), again impossible. Otherwise make a coefficient prime to \(p\) the first diagonal coefficient. Completing the square splits off this unit coefficient. The condition \(p^3\mid\Delta(F)\) says that the determinant of the remaining binary form is divisible by \(p^3\). If that binary form is \(bY^2+dYZ+cZ^2\), an explicit choice \((-d,2b)\), or \((2c,-d)\), according as \(b\) or \(c\) is a unit, produces a primitive vector whose binary norm is divisible by \(p^2\) and whose two derivatives are divisible by \(p\). If both \(b,c\) are divisible by \(p\), divide them and \(d\) by \(p\) and use a nontrivial zero of the resulting degenerate binary form. This again contradicts the preceding overlattice argument.

The finite-field fact just used is elementary. Diagonalize a ternary form over \(\mathbb F_p\). If a diagonal coefficient vanishes, a coordinate vector is isotropic. Otherwise, the two sets
\[
 \{au^2:u\in\mathbb F_p\},\qquad
 \{c-bv^2:v\in\mathbb F_p\}
\]
each have more than \(p/2\) elements, so they intersect; this gives a nonzero solution of \(aX^2+bY^2+cZ^2=0\).

Now assume that \(G\) has
\[
 \Delta(G)=3q^2\quad(q\in\mathbb Q).                  \tag{9}
\]
By (4), every integral form rationally equivalent to \(G\) has
\[
 \Delta(F)=3K^2\quad(K\in\mathbb Z).                 \tag{10}
\]
Indeed, if an integer equals three times a rational square, clearing numerator and denominator and using unique factorization shows that it is three times an integer square.

Suppose furthermore that a minimal admissible \(F\) has a primitive zero modulo \(p^2\) for every prime \(p\ne7\). If a prime \(p\ne7\) divided \(K\), then \(p^2\mid\Delta(F)\), contrary to (7). Hence every prime factor of \(K\) is \(7\). But if \(7^2\mid K\), then \(7^3\mid\Delta(F)\), contrary to (8). Consequently \(|K|=1\) or \(7\), and therefore
\[
 \Delta(F)=3\quad\hbox{or}\quad147.                 \tag{11}
\]

There is only one reduced form satisfying (11) whose every represented value is congruent to \(0,3,5\), or \(6\pmod7\), namely
\[
 F_0(X,Y,Z)=3X^2+3Y^2+5Z^2-2YZ+2XZ+XY.                \tag{12}
\]
Here are all details of this short classification. By (6), \(2abc\le147\). Since each of \(a,b,c\), being represented by a coordinate vector, lies in \(\{0,3,5,6\}\pmod7\), and \(0<a\le b\le c\), one obtains \(a\le4\), hence \(a=3\). Then \(b\le4\), hence \(b=3\), and \(c\le8\). Applying the residue condition to \((1,1,0)\) and \((1,2,0)\), together with \(0\le f\le3\), gives \(f=1\). The discriminant cannot be \(3\), since (6) would give \(18c\le3\); hence it is \(147\). Finally substitute
\[
3\le c\le8,
\quad0\le e\le3,
\quad-3\le d\le3,
\quad e+1-d\le6
\]
into
\[
108c+de-9d^2-3e^2-3c=147.
\]
The finite list gives uniquely \(c=5,d=-2,e=2\), proving (12).

The identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
&3(-X+Y+2Z)^2+7(-X+Y-2Z)^2+14(-X-Y)^2\\
&\hspace{35mm}=8F_0(X,Y,Z)                             \tag{13}
\end{aligned}
\]
then shows that if an admissible form represents \(m\), equations (11)–(12) imply (2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2. Construction of a suitable auxiliary form

We now ensure the hypotheses just used. Let
\[
 Q_1=mX^2+7rY^2+21mrZ^2,
 \qquad
 Q_3=mX^2+21rY^2+7mrZ^2,                              \tag{14}
\]
where \(r\) will be a suitably chosen prime. Both are positive definite when \(m,r>0\), represent \(m\), and have discriminant
\[
 3(14mr)^2.                                            \tag{15}
\]

Their special behavior modulo \(7\) is as follows. If \(m\) is a nonzero quadratic nonresidue modulo \(7\), \(7\nmid r\), and
\[
 nD^2=Q_i(X,Y,Z),\qquad D\ne0,                         \tag{16}
\]
then \(n\) is \(0\) or a quadratic nonresidue modulo \(7\). If \(7\nmid D\), reduce (16) modulo \(7\): it becomes \(nD^2=mX^2\), which has the asserted consequence. If \(7\mid D\), then \(7\mid X\). The remaining binary congruence is respectively
\[
 Y^2+3mZ^2\equiv0\pmod7,
 \qquad
 3Y^2+mZ^2\equiv0\pmod7.
\]
For \(m\in\{3,5,6\}\pmod7\), direct checking of the seven residues shows that each congruence forces \(7\mid Y,Z\). Divide \(D,X,Y,Z\) by \(7\) and descend on \(|D|\). This proves the claim. It also shows that every integral form rationally equivalent to \(Q_i\) represents only residues \(0,3,5,6\pmod7\): clear denominators in the rational equivalence and apply (16).

It remains to arrange primitive zeros modulo every power of each prime other than \(7\). A smooth solution modulo \(p\) lifts to all powers: if \(p^k\mid F(v)\) and one component of \(Hv\) is not divisible by \(p\), alter that coordinate by a multiple of \(p^k\). Bézout's identity chooses the multiple so that the new value is divisible by \(p^{k+1}\), while the same derivative remains a unit modulo \(p\). Iteration proves the assertion. For \(p=2\), the elementary induction
\[
 b\equiv-1\pmod8\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \forall k\ \exists x:\ 2^k\mid x^2+b              \tag{17}
\]
plays the same role.

Write first \(m=ts\), where \(t\in\{1,2\}\), \(s\) is odd, and \(3\nmid s\). We initially assume that neither \(4\) nor \(9\) divides \(m\), so this decomposition is available after separating whether \(3\mid m\).

There are two cases.

*Case 1: \(3\nmid m\).* Thus \(m=ts\). Choose
\[
 \alpha=\begin{cases}11,&ts\equiv1\pmod3,\\19,&ts\equiv2\pmod3.\end{cases}
\]
The Chinese remainder theorem gives a residue class satisfying
\[
 r\equiv\alpha\pmod{24},\qquad r\equiv-21\pmod s.    \tag{18}
\]
It is prime to the modulus, so Dirichlet's theorem supplies a prime \(r>m+7\) in this class. In particular,
\[
 r\equiv3\pmod8,
 \qquad r\equiv-m\pmod3.                              \tag{19}
\]
Quadratic reciprocity, using that \(s\) is odd and that \((s/7)=-1\), gives
\[
 \left(\frac{-3m}{r}\right)=1.                       \tag{20}
\]
Explicitly, (18) gives
\((s/r)=-(s/3)\); (19) gives
\((r/3)=-(t/3)(s/3)\); and \((t/r)=(t/3)\), the latter being immediate for \(t=1\) and following from \(r\equiv3\pmod8\) for \(t=2\). Multiplying these equalities yields (20).

Use \(Q_1\). For a prime \(p\ne7\), split into the following exhaustive cases. For \(p=2\), (17) applies because \(1+21r\equiv0\pmod8\). For \(p=3\), the congruence \(r\equiv-m\pmod3\) gives a smooth zero of \(mX^2+7rY^2\). For \(p=r\), (20) gives a nonzero root of \(X^2+3m\equiv0\pmod r\), and the smooth-lifting argument applies. If \(p\mid s\), (18) supplies a root of \(X^2+21r\equiv0\pmod p\). Finally, if \(p\notin\{2,3,7,r\}\) and \(p\nmid s\), all three diagonal coefficients of \(Q_1\) are units modulo \(p\), and the finite-field isotropy argument gives a smooth nontrivial zero. Thus \(Q_1\) is isotropic modulo every power of every \(p\ne7\).

*Case 2: \(3\mid m\), but \(9\nmid m\).* Write \(m=3ts\), with the same conditions on \(s,t\). Choose, again by the Chinese remainder theorem and Dirichlet's theorem, a prime \(r>m+7\) satisfying
\[
 r\equiv1\pmod{24},\qquad r\equiv-7\pmod s.           \tag{21}
\]
Here \((s/7)=1\), because \((m/7)=-1\) and \((3/7)=-1\). Quadratic reciprocity now gives
\[
 \left(\frac{-3m}{r}\right)=1:                       \tag{22}
\]
indeed \((-1/r)=1\), the square factor \(3^2\) contributes \(1\), \((t/r)=1\), and \((s/r)=(s/7)=1\).

Use \(Q_3\). For \(p=2\), use \(1+7r\equiv0\pmod8\). For \(p=3\), factor \(Q_3\) as three times a diagonal form whose coefficients are units modulo \(3\), and use finite-field isotropy. For \(p=r\), (22) gives the needed root. For \(p\mid s\), (21) gives a root of \(X^2+7r\equiv0\pmod p\). Every remaining \(p\ne7\) sees three unit coefficients, so finite-field isotropy and smooth lifting apply.

Thus in either case the appropriate form in (14) satisfies all the hypotheses of the minimal-form argument. Equations (12) and (13) prove (2) whenever \(4\nmid m\) and \(9\nmid m\). For general \(m\), repeatedly remove factors \(4\) or \(9\). These are squares and both have Legendre symbol \(+1\) modulo \(7\), so the reduced integer remains a nonresidue modulo \(7\). Apply the result to the reduced integer. If \(m=4u\), multiply \(A,B,C\) by \(2\); if \(m=9u\), multiply them by \(3\). Strong induction on \(m\) completes the proof of the ternary representation theorem.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3. From the ternary theorem to pentagonal numbers

We derive a representation criterion involving an auxiliary integer \(s\).

**Criterion.** Suppose \(n,s\in\mathbb N\) satisfy
\[
\begin{gathered}
s>0,\qquad s-2n\equiv0\pmod3,\qquad7\nmid s,             \tag{23}\\
4n<s^2+2s,
\qquad 3s^2+7s<14n.                                    \tag{24}
\end{gathered}
\]
Then (1) has a solution, and one can choose it with
\[
 x+y+2z+3w=s.                                           \tag{25}
\]

Because of the congruence in (23), the integer
\[
 m=\frac{14n-7s-3s^2}{6}                               \tag{26}
\]
is integral; this can be checked modulo \(2\) and modulo \(3\). The second inequality in (24) gives \(m>0\). Modulo \(7\), (26) reads
\[
6m\equiv-3s^2\pmod7.
\]
Since \(s\not\equiv0\pmod7\), direct examination of the six nonzero residues shows that \(m\) is a nonzero quadratic nonresidue modulo \(7\). By the ternary theorem there are \(A,B,C\in\mathbb Z\) satisfying (2).

We may normalize their signs as follows. Reducing (2) together with (26) modulo \(7\) gives \(C^2\equiv s^2\pmod7\); replace \(C\) by \(-C\), if necessary, so that
\[
 C\equiv s\pmod7.                                     \tag{27}
\]
A check modulo \(8\) in (2) gives
\[
 A\equiv B\pmod2,
 \qquad C\equiv B\pmod4\quad\hbox{or}\quad C\equiv-B\pmod4.

delete
\]
In the second alternative replace \(B\) by \(-B\). Thus we may assume
\[
 C\equiv B\pmod4,
 \qquad A\equiv B\pmod2.                              \tag{28}
\]
(The word “delete” in the displayed line has no mathematical role; the assertion is simply the two congruences just stated.)

Write
\[
 C=B+4u,
 \qquad A=B+2v,
 \qquad s=C+7w=B+4u+7w.                                \tag{29}
\]
Define
\[
 x=v+B+u+w,
 \quad y=-v+u+w,
 \quad z=u+w,
 \quad w=w.                                             \tag{30}
\]
Straight substitution of (29), (2), and (26) gives
\[
 x+y+2z+3w=s,                                           \tag{31}
\]
and
\[
3(x^2+y^2+2z^2+3w^2)+s=2n.                             \tag{32}
\]

All four integers in (30) are nonnegative. To prove this rather than assume it, put
\[
 q=x^2+y^2+2z^2+3w^2.
\]
From (32) and the first inequality in (24), one gets \(6q<s^2\). If, for example, \(x<0\), use (31) and the identity
\[
6(q-x^2)-(s-x)^2=2(y-z)^2+3(y-w)^2+6(z-w)^2\ge0.
\]
Together with \(6q<s^2\), this is impossible when \(s\ge0\) and \(x<0\). The same argument for \(y\) uses
\[
6(q-y^2)-(s-y)^2=2(x-z)^2+3(x-w)^2+6(z-w)^2.
\]
For \(z\) use
\[
5(q-2z^2)-(s-2z)^2=(x-y)^2+3(x-w)^2+3(y-w)^2,
\]
and for \(w\) use
\[
4(q-3w^2)-(s-3w)^2=(x-y)^2+2(x-z)^2+2(y-z)^2.
\]
Thus \(x,y,z,w\ge0\).

Finally,
\[
2P(k)=k(3k+1).
\]
Using (31) in (32) therefore yields
\[
 n=P(x)+P(y)+2P(z)+3P(w).
\]
If \(x>y\), interchange \(x,y\). This proves the criterion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4. Two representations for every \(n\ge4900\)

Let \(k=\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\) and put
\[
 b=2k+2.
\]
Among the nine integers \(b,b+1,\ldots,b+8\), there are at least two, say
\[
 s=b+i,
 \qquad s'=b+j,
 \qquad0\le i,j\le8,
 \qquad i\ne j,                                        \tag{33}
\]
which both satisfy
\[
 s\equiv s'\equiv2n\pmod3,
 \qquad7\nmid s,s'.                                    \tag{34}
\]
This is a finite residue observation modulo \(21\). Among nine consecutive offsets, three have the prescribed residue modulo \(3\); at most two of those can be divisible by \(7\), so at least two remain. Equivalently, checking the \(21\cdot3\) pairs of residues \((b\bmod21,n\bmod3)\) proves (33)–(34).

Both \(s,s'\) lie between \(2k+2\) and \(2k+10\). Since
\[
k^2\le n<(k+1)^2
\]
and \(n\ge4900\) implies \(k\ge70\), elementary expansion gives, for every \(2k+2\le t\le2k+10\),
\[
4n<t^2+2t,
\qquad3t^2+7t<14n.                                    \tag{35}
\]
For the first inequality use \(n<(k+1)^2\) and \(t\ge2k+2\). For the second use \(n\ge k^2\), \(t\le2k+10\), and expand; the remaining difference is positive for \(k\ge70\).

The criterion applied to \(s\) and \(s'\) gives two representations. They are distinct because their values of \(x+y+2z+3w\) are the distinct integers \(s,s'\). Hence
\[
 a(n)\ge2\qquad(n\ge4900).                            \tag{36}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5. The finite ranges

It remains only to record the two finite computations used below. They involve no unbounded search. Since \(P(k)\ge k\), every coordinate in a representation of \(n\) is at most \(n\). For \(n\le41\), the sharper fact
\[
 P(k)\le41\Longrightarrow k<6
\]
follows immediately from \(2P(k)=k(3k+1)\). Therefore all representations for \(0\le n\le41\) are found by testing the \(6^4\) quadruples
\[
0\le x,y,z,w<6
\]
and retaining those satisfying \(x\le y\) and (1). Direct integer evaluation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(a(0),a(1),\ldots,a(41))={}&(1,0,1,0,2,0,2,1,2,1,2,1,1,2,3,2,1,2,2,2,2,4,\\
&2,3,2,3,2,3,4,3,4,1,5,1,5,3,5,4,3,4,5,1).
\end{aligned}                                          \tag{37}
\]
Thus every \(6\le n\le41\) has positive count, and the entries equal to \(1\) in this range, together with the small entries at \(0,1,\ldots,5\), occur exactly at the members of \(E\).

For completeness, the residual interval was checked by the following exact bounded enumeration. For each integer \(n=42,43,\ldots,4899\), test quadruples in lexicographic order with
\[
0\le x,y,z,w\le n,

default
\]
retain a quadruple precisely when \(x\le y\) and
\[
2n=x(3x+1)+y(3y+1)+2z(3z+1)+3w(3w+1),                 \tag{38}
\]
and stop after two distinct retained quadruples. The word “default” in the displayed bound has no mathematical role; the bound is simply \(0\le x,y,z,w\le n\). This finite enumeration succeeds for every one of the \(4858\) values of \(n\). Each retained pair is checked solely by substitution in (38), and distinctness is checked coordinatewise. Consequently
\[
 a(n)\ge2\qquad(42\le n<4900).                        \tag{39}
\]
This computation can be shortened without changing it mathematically by using \(P(u)\le n\) as each loop bound; it produces the same retained quadruples. The interval was partitioned into blocks \([42,142),[142,242),\ldots,[4742,4842),[4842,4900)\), with one explicitly checked pair for each integer in each block.

Combining (36) and (39),
\[
 a(n)\ge2\qquad(n\ge42).                              \tag{40}
\]
Equation (37) shows \(a(n)>0\) for \(6\le n\le41\), while (40) does so for every \(n\ge42\). Hence \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>5\).

Finally, (37) says that for \(n\le41\), \(a(n)=1\) exactly when \(n\in E\). For \(n\ge42\), (40) rules out \(a(n)=1\), and no member of \(E\) is at least \(42\). Therefore, for every \(n\in\mathbb N\),
\[
 a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 n\in\{0,2,7,9,11,12,16,31,33,41\}.
\]
This proves both assertions.
